newsitem.title: USA: Ecuador to intervene in Texaco enviro case.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador to intervene in Texaco enviro case.

text.p: The Ecuadoran government plans to intervene Friday in a class-action lawsuit against Texaco Inc for alleged environmental damage during the company's 28-year tenure in the Andean country, a lawyer representing the government said Wednesday.
A U.S. district court judge dismissed the case last week contending that the U.S. is not the appropriate forum for the suit.

"We're going to intervene which will allow the plaintiffs to file a motion for reconsideration," said Henry Dahl, a Dallas lawyer who represents the Ecuadoran government. "This is the first time a foreign state intervenes in this type of case."
Dahl said Ecuador's state oil company Petroecuador might join the intervention.

In last week's U.S. ruling in White Plains, New York, Judge Jed Rakoff said another cause for dismissal was the plaintiffs' failure to bring the case against the Ecuadoran government and Petroecuador, along with Texaco, as they also participated in the operations that allegedly led to the environmental damage.
In his ruling, the judge said the Ecuadoran government had issued conflicting opinions on the case through statements by various officials.
"If the government of Ecuador expressed unequivocal support in favor of the lawsuit, Rakoff could and should change his mind," one of the plaintiffs' lawyers said.
If the judge doesn't agree to reconsider, the plaintiffs would appeal, Dahl said.

A Texaco spokesman reiterated the company's position that the case belongs in Ecuador. "The Ecuadoran government is a sovereign entity and is within its rights to do as it pleases, but our position remains that this is a matter that should be resolved in Ecuador."

"You see all the problems Texaco has had in the U.S. courts lately, it's no wonder they want to go to a foreign court," Dahl said, referring to the oil company's recent settlement of a race bias lawsuit in New York.
Texaco operated in Ecuador from 1964 to 1992, producing a peak of 220,000 barrels per day of oil.
In 1994, the company signed an accord to shut abandoned wells and pits, and revegetate affected land. That program is now "95 percent complete," a Texaco spokesman said.

The first case against Texaco for alleged environmental damage in Ecuador was filed in August 1993, and was subsequently dismissed on the same grounds that the U.S. is not the appropriate venue for the suit.
